newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Pre-holiday data feast.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Pre-holiday data feast.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will sit down to a pre-Thanksgiving data feast on Wednesday, as players gobble up a virtual smorgasbord of economic releases.
The U.S. Treasury and related debt markets will close at 1400 EST/1900 GMT on Wednesday ahead of the Thanksgiving Day holiday. There will be no trading on Thursday.
Friday will also be a shortened session, with dealings again ending at 1400 EST/1900 GMT. Full trading will resume on Monday, December 2.

"We've got a double header and then a quadruple header," said Carey Leahey, vice president and senior financial markets economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, referring to two economic reports set for release at 0830 EST/1330 GMT and four releases due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

At the earlier hour, the market will whet its appetite with first-time claims for unemployment benefits in the week ended November 23, and devour the Commerce Department's second estimate of third-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Claims are expected to total 336,000 compared to 344,000 in the prior week, according to a Reuters poll.
GDP is projected to have grown at a 1.7-percent pace in the third quarter, compared with a 2.2-percent rate in the Commerce Department's first estimate released last month.
Experts said a GDP growth rate with a "one handle," although widely anticipated, should be favorably received by the Treasury market.

At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, players will snack on consumer sentiment from the University of Michigan, and the October Help-Wanted Advertising Index from The Conference Board before relishing the piece de resistance -- the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index (PMI).
"From a trading perspective, Chicago PMI will be the most important," Leahey said, noting the regional industrial index has been running consistently ahead of the national gauge.

Leahey said no hard and fast reasons exist as to why the Chicago PMI has been outperforming the National Association of Purchasing Management's monthly index. However, "Given what the 30-year (bond) has been doing lately, the Chicago PMI could kick the market around certainly more than the (data) series is worth," he added.
Experts forecast a reading of 55.1 for November's Chicago PMI compared with 56.9 in October.
The second most savory piece of data set for release at 1000 EST/1500 GMT is durable goods, analysts said.
Data on big-ticket items are typically released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, but the figures will be issued by Commerce at the later time this month only.

Analysts predicted a 2.0-percent decline in orders versus a meaty 4.9-percent jump the prior month. Excluding the defense component, orders are seen down 2.2 percent compared to a 4.8-percent rise in September.
A recent strike at General Motors Corp was the main reason behind the expected slump in durables.
Analysts said an even sharper drop than the 2.0-percent slide expected, however, will probably be discounted by the market as a one-time, strike-induced distortion.
On the flip-side, Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc, said any pop in orders could debunk perceptions that the fourth quarter may be sluggish.
"We had a good reading (on durables) in September and if we get another good reading, that could begin to alter perceptions about the fourth quarter," Moran said.
"The perception is beginning to emerge that the fourth quarter will be weak," he added.
Still, Moran said he is expecting a 1.5-percent slide in orders partly due to the GM strike and partly as an offset to the strength in commercial aircraft seen in September.
Finally, the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index is expected to print 98.0 in the final November report versus 96.5 in the final October release.
"Michigan will be uneventful," one analyst said.
